headline: Public hearings on new training center at 511 Maine Avenue and lot subdivision at 6 Bangor Mall Boulevard.
summary: The board will hold public hearings on a land development permit for a 6,070 sq. ft. training center and cold storage building renovation at 511 Maine Avenue, and on a minor subdivision and planned group development at 6 Bangor Mall Boulevard. The board will also discuss a proposed growth boundary change, a workshop on removing floor area ratio restrictions in the Downtown Development District, and updates on the Land Use Plan.

Treatment measures 
To provide the required treatment as required by Chapter 500, Section C General Standards, a vegetated 
soil filter is proposed.  This vegetated soil filter will detain a runoff volume equal to 1.0 inch of the runoff from 
the impervious area runoff plus 0.4 inch of the runoff from the landscaped area draining to it.  
The areas draining to the vegetated soil filter are shown on plan sheet C6 STORMWATER MANAGEMENT, 
included with this submittal.   No runoff from areas outside of the re-development area are directed to the 
soil filter basin.  The sizing of the vegetated filter basin is shown in the portion of the spreadsheet included 
below: The treatment and surface area provided exceeds the minimum required.  A valve and orifice disc 
will be provided to restrict the outflow so that the treatment time within the filter is at least 24 hours.  
Although this project does not use  Low Impact Development credits to reduce the size of the treatment 
volume, several Low Impact Development strateg ies are incorporated into the design of the site to meet 
the intent of the Maine DEP Chapter 500 Low Impact Development mandates.   These measures provide 
several benefits that enhance the quality and quantity of the stormwater resulting from the development on 
the site.    
Careful consideration of the layout of the parking, drives, buildings and infrastructure on the site resulted in 
a design that allowed clean roof runoff and runoff from existing impervious areas  to be hydraulically 
separated from the area of the site being treated by the new soil filter; reducing the footprint of the treatment 
structure.  This design also allows runoff from the new parking and drive areas to drain naturally across the 
curbless edges, lessening the need for additional catch basins and closed storm drai ns that prod uce 
concentrated flows.  The sequential treatment process (train) including over land flow through  the stone 
shoulder prior to entering the filter basin is a LID strategy aimed at slowing runoff, preventing clogging of 
the treatment area and extending the life of the filtration media. 
The landscaped areas, including the mitigation areas on the site, are to be planted with native landscaping 
that will also reduce impact and improve water quality of runoff from the development on the site.  Native 
seeding and landscaping that requires minimal maintenance helps to naturally maintain soil permeability, 
absorb nutrients (nitrogen/phosphorus), and facilitate evapotranspiration without the need for high 
maintenance, fertilizers, or pesticides.

Regarding: Proposed growth boundary change 
The VA is interested in putting a new VA hospital at the two parcels at the corner of Stillwater Avenue and 
Kittredge Road, R60-12-C and R60-011-D. A map of the parcels (outlined in cyan) is shown below, along with 
the zoning and current growth boundary (shown by the thick black line). The parcel to the west, R60-011-D, is 
outside the growth boundary and is zoned RR&A. RR&A would not currently allow a hospital, so a zone 
change would be needed.  
For newer members, the Growth Boundary is a distinct boundary under the state’s Growth Management 
statute that establishes the area in a municipality where said city/town will seek to direct growth.  Directing 
growth can take the form of more dense or more uses allowed in zoning, allowance of TIF districts and other 
development incentives.  The boundary typically follows the area where services are readily available, as in 
roads, utilities, and public safety.  Recent changes to housing legislation has given more focus on where the 
growth boundary is located because higher densities are now required for areas within the growth boundary.  
The growth boundary is set during the Comprehensive Plan (specifically the Land Use Plan) process by 
design; it is important to have a comprehensive look at your municipality in order to fully develop where the 
growth boundary should be located.   
It is not typically recommended to change a property to a more intense, commercial zone where the current 
land use plan shows it being both rural residential and outside the growth area. Therefore, the cleaner option 
would be to change the growth boundary to encompass the lot that’s currently outside of it. As the Committee 
may know, staff is working on a complete code and zoning map update as implementation of the Land Use 
Plan. Normally we would encompass this change as part of that work but there is timeliness to this request for 
consideration as the developers of the VA hospital are looking to move forward with their plans.  We 
anticipated some edge modifications to the growth boundary when we prepared the proposed Land Use Plan.  
Often circumstances change in the City and modifications may make sense where there is water and sewer 
infrastructure or if other development priorities come to light.  You can look at the Comprehensive Plan and the 
Land Use Plan here:  https://bangormaine.gov/474/City-Plans  
In this case, sewer is available to the eastern parcel, so it could easily be pulled to the western parcel, 
particularly if a building traverses both lots.  A hospital/medical clinic is also a use that will have different peak 
traffic needs than the heavy traffic from retail uses prevalent in the area.  The use of a VA hospital is in keeping 
with the Economic Development strategy in fostering and supporting medical uses. 
Staff would like Council direction on if this change is desired; we will also be meeting with the Planning Board 
to discuss this adjustment. This process should not be seen as connected to the process underway to update 
the City’s land development code and zoning; any changes to the growth boundary should be seen as an 
amendment to the Comprehensive Plan and would have to go through the same adoption process. That 
process is a public hearing with the Planning Board with at least 30-day’s notice given and a final vote by the 
Council.

Regarding: Floor area ratio (FAR) removal from the Downtown Development District (DDD) 
This memo outlines the proposed removal of the floor area ratio (FAR) from the Downtown Development 
District (DDD). A need has been expressed to create more flexibility for expanding businesses and residences 
downtown. The floor area ratio in Downtown Development District can hinder infill development. Once the 
maximum floor area ratio is met on a lot, no additional floor area may be added.  
Floor area ratio is the floor area of a building on a lot divided by the horizontal area of the lot. A building with 
40,000sqft of floor area on a 10,000 square foot lot has a FAR of 4.0. A building with 10,000sqft of floor area 
on a 40,000sqft lot has a FAR of 0.25.  
Floor area ratio (FAR) is an outdated control and staff will be recommending removal of this control in the new 
Land Development Code. However, this current proposed text amendment will only remove it from the 
Downtown Development District (DDD) since new development is proposed there that would be limited by this. 
FAR was used to control building bulk and volume in the early to mid-20th century. When FARs were 
implemented around the country, some of the perceived benefits were protecting sunlight, neighborhood 
character, and infrastructure capacity, most of which do not hold true today. 
FAR does not necessarily protect sunlight or neighborhood character because it does not consider how 
buildings are designed or positioned and the heights of them. Additionally, floor area is not a good measure to 
ensure infrastructure capacity. A multi-unit residential development and commercial development both with 
40,000sqft of floor area will have different levels of usage and impacts on infrastructure. The City also has to 
ensure that all developments have adequate infrastructure capacity through other standards in the Ordinance. 
Some of the most well-known historic buildings downtown already exceed this standard. For example, the 
Graham Building where the Rudman Winchell offices are has a FAR of approximately 4.5 and the Eastern 
Trust building at 6 State Street has a FAR of about 5.3. 
The proposed amendments align with policy recommendations 1 and 7 in the 2022 Comprehensive Plan 
regarding encouraging development in the growth boundary and increasing housing supply downtown by 
revising zoning regulations. 
The proposed language is included in your packets and will also be on the October 6th Planning Board agenda 
for the Board’s feedback. If Councilors and Planning Board are amenable, staff will forward the formal 
language through for adoption.
